modules.name: Events
modules.header:
Reading a document as a stream of events, without building a tree.
A tree is convenient and it is also what makes a large document expensive. Streaming trades random access for
constant memory: events arrive in document order, once, and the caller keeps only what it wants. A program
reading one setting out of a large configuration file never allocates for the rest of it.
What a streaming reader cannot do is notice that a table was defined twice, because knowing that requires
remembering every table already seen — which is the tree it was trying not to build. So this checks syntax
and structure and nothing else, and a caller that needs TOML's redefinition rules enforced wants the parser.
Saying so here is better than a reader that quietly accepts a document the parser would refuse.
Text is left as it was written, escapes and all. Resolving them costs an allocation, and a caller skipping a
field should not pay for the field it is skipping; `TomlDecodeText` is there for the ones it keeps.

modules.name: Lexer
modules.header:
Turning TOML text into tokens, with the position of each one.
TOML has more lexical surface than JSON and almost all of it is string and number forms. There are four ways
to write a string — basic, multi-line basic, literal, multi-line literal — and they differ in whether
escapes are honoured and whether newlines are allowed, which is exactly the sort of distinction an
implementation collapses and then surprises someone whose Windows path lost its backslashes.
Spans are carried on every token because TOML is a configuration format, and a configuration error that does
not say where it is costs more than the parse itself. Every diagnostic this package produces can point at a
line and column because the token knew.

modules.name: Parser
modules.header:
Building a document from tokens, and refusing the three different ways of defining a table twice.
Most of a TOML parser is bookkeeping about tables. `[a.b]` creates `a` implicitly and `b` deliberately, and
what may happen to each of them afterwards is different: a later `[a]` is fine because `a` was only implied,
while a later `[a.b]` is a redefinition. A table written inline is closed the moment its brace shuts, and one
reached through a dotted key is closed as soon as the line ends. Three rules, three reasons, three separate
errors — because "duplicate key" tells a writer nothing about which of them they broke.
The recursion of inline tables and arrays is bounded by the depth limit rather than by the stack, checked
before descending, so a document built to exhaust the stack is refused while there is still stack to refuse
it with.
What this produces is a tree of values and nothing else. Comments are skipped by the lexer and never arrive
here, so no amount of care further down could keep them; the same goes for blank lines, for indentation, and
for whether a number was written in hexadecimal. Reading a document and writing it back gives an equivalent
document, not the same file, and this package is not the one to reach for when the file belongs to someone
else.

modules.name: Scalar
modules.header:
Turning a scalar token's text into a value, with TOML's grammar applied rather than assumed.
Every rule here is one a permissive reader would let through and a strict one would not: an underscore has to
sit between two digits, a decimal integer may not carry a leading zero, a float needs digits on both sides of
its point. None of that is decoration. `010` meaning eight to one reader and ten to another is how a port
number becomes the wrong port number, and TOML's answer is that it means neither — it is simply not a TOML
integer, and saying so is the job of this file.
Each refusal says where. A scalar is short, so a reader given only "malformed" has to find the offending
character themselves — and the reader most often given one is a person looking at a configuration file that
stopped a program starting. The offsets are into the scalar's own text, counted in bytes from its first
character, and the parser adds the token's own position to reach a line and a column in the document.
Getting that right takes one piece of bookkeeping: underscores are stripped before the digits are checked, so
an offset into the stripped text is not an offset into what the caller wrote. `Stripped` keeps, for each byte
it copies, where that byte came from, and every offset reported below is mapped back through it. `1_0_x0` must
point at the `x`, not at the fourth character of something the caller never saw.

modules.name: Value
modules.header:
What a TOML value is, and what a table remembers about how it was made.
TOML has real types where JSON has one number and a great deal of hope: an integer is an integer, a float is a
float, and a date is a date. That is most of what makes TOML pleasant to write configuration in, and it is why
a value here carries a `Date` and a `TimeOfDay` from `Time` rather than the text it was written with.
A table also remembers how it came to exist. TOML forbids defining the same table twice, and forbids adding to
one that was written inline or reached through a dotted key — three different mistakes with three different
reasons. The flags below are what let the parser say which one happened instead of reporting a duplicate and
leaving the writer to work out why.

modules.name: Writer
modules.header:
Writing a document back out, deterministically.
The same tree always produces the same bytes. That is not an aesthetic preference: configuration files live in
version control, and a writer whose output depends on hash order or on how the tree was built produces a diff
every time it runs, which trains everyone to stop reading the diffs.
So entries are written in the order the table holds them, keys are bare whenever TOML allows a bare key and
quoted otherwise, and strings are always basic strings. A writer that guessed between the four string forms
would produce output that changed shape when a value gained a backslash, which is the sort of churn nobody
asked for; a basic string is always valid and always round-trips.
Tables are written as headers rather than inline, except inside an array where TOML offers no other spelling.
A document written, read and written again produces the same bytes the second time.
What this cannot do is reproduce a file. The tree has no comments in it, no blank lines, and no memory of
whether a number was written in hexadecimal or a string in a literal form, so the output is the writer's
layout of the same values rather than the layout it was read from. That is fine for generating configuration
and for writing back a file this program owns; running it over a file someone else wrote and hand-formatted
will produce a diff of the whole file.
Failures are the ones every writer in this workspace reports, so a document goes into anything a `TextWriter`
reaches with no translation at the seam. What the destination said travels unchanged: a buffer that is merely
full reports `InsufficientCapacity` and a stream that has died reports `WriterFailure`, where the status this
replaced had one case, `Failed`, standing for both — and a caller who could have written the document somewhere
larger had no way to know that was the problem. A header path that will not fit the buffer is `ValueOutOfRange`,
which is what that case is for: the document is good and the form asked for cannot hold it.

Decodes a text token's span into an owned string, honouring the escapes its form allows.
A literal string is copied unchanged — that is what makes it the right form for a Windows path — while a
basic string has its escapes resolved, including the line-ending backslash that lets a multi-line string be
wrapped in the source without the wrapping appearing in the value.

doc.summary: Why parsing stopped.
doc.markdown:
Why parsing stopped.
Failure-only: a parse that did not stop hands back a document instead. The distinctions between the four
table-definition cases are the ones worth keeping — `DuplicateKey`, `RedefinedTable`, `ExtendedInlineTable`
and `ExtendedDottedTable` are four different mistakes with four different fixes, and a reader told only that
a key was defined twice would have to work out which rule they had met.
The two cases that have something more to say carry it rather than reporting it beside themselves, so a caller
holding the failure cannot be holding half of one.

cases.name: Lexical
cases.doc: The lexer refused the input, for the reason carried.

cases.name: Unexpected
cases.doc: A token that cannot appear where it did.

cases.name: Truncated
cases.doc: The document ended in the middle of something.

cases.name: DuplicateKey
cases.doc: A key given a value twice in the same table.

cases.name: RedefinedTable
cases.doc: A table defined by a header that had already been defined by one.

cases.name: ExtendedInlineTable
cases.doc: An attempt to add to a table that was written inline, which its closing brace ended.

cases.name: ExtendedDottedTable
cases.doc: An attempt to add to a table that a dotted key created, which its line ended.

cases.name: NotATable
cases.doc: A key path that runs through something that is not a table.

cases.name: NotATableArray
cases.doc: A `[[name]]` header naming an array that was not built from headers, or a table.

cases.name: BadValue
cases.doc:
A scalar whose text is not the number or date TOML's grammar defines, for the reason carried. The scalar
failure's own offset is into the scalar's text; the failure around it is positioned in the document.

cases.name: BadText
cases.doc: A string whose escapes name no scalar value.

cases.name: TooDeep
cases.doc: Values nested deeper than the limit allowed.

cases.name: OutOfMemory
cases.doc: The allocator refused.

doc.summary: Reads the whole document into a table.
doc.markdown:
Reads the whole document into a table.
On failure the table holds whatever had been read before the refusal, and `Outcome` says what stopped it
and where. A partial document is not a usable one; it is returned rather than discarded so a caller can
show what was understood before the line that was not.
What comes back is the values and nothing else. Comments never reach the parser, and neither does the
blank line someone put between two sections or the fact that a number was written in hexadecimal. This
reads configuration; it does not edit files.
doc.returns: the document, or the failure and where it was found

doc.summary: Reads `input` into a table, or says why it could not and where.
doc.markdown:
Reads `input` into a table, or says why it could not and where.
A refusal gives back no document at all. Whatever had been read when the parser stopped is released here,
which is the only place it can be done once — and handing it back would be worse than useless, because a
program configured from half a file runs with some settings applied and some defaulted.
Fails with any case of `TomlParseError`, positioned at the byte, line and column where parsing stopped.
doc.returns: the document, or the failure that stopped it

doc.summary: Why a scalar could not be read, and where in it.
doc.markdown:
Why a scalar could not be read, and where in it.
Failure-only: there is no case meaning nothing went wrong, because a scalar that read hands back its value
instead. Every offset is a zero-based byte offset into the scalar's own text, as the caller wrote it —
underscores included — and reachable through `Text::ParseFailure`.

cases.name: Malformed
cases.doc:
The text does not have the shape TOML defines, at the byte carried. That is the first character that
cannot be part of what was being read: a digit the base does not have, a point with nothing after it, an
underscore that is not between two digits, or the end of the text when it stops early.

cases.name: OutOfRange
cases.doc:
The value is outside what an `int64`, a `float64` or the calendar can hold. The offset is the start of the
text, since it is the whole value that does not fit rather than any one character of it.

cases.name: TooLong
cases.doc: The text is longer than any TOML scalar needs. The offset is the first character past the bound.

items.name: TomlParseInteger
items.signature: pub func TomlParseInteger(text: char8[..]) -> int64 ! TomlScalarError

doc.summary: Reads an integer, in any of the four bases TOML writes.
doc.markdown:
Reads an integer, in any of the four bases TOML writes.
A leading zero is refused for a decimal integer, because `010` is eight in one language and ten in another
and TOML declines to pick: it is not an integer at all. A sign is refused on a based integer for the same
reason — the grammar does not offer one, so accepting it would be inventing a dialect.
`Malformed` at the first character that cannot be part of the integer, `TooLong` past the length bound, and
`OutOfRange` at the start when the digits are a number `int64` cannot hold. Every offset is into `text` as
written, underscores included.
doc.returns: the integer, or why it could not be read and where

items.name: TomlParseFloat
items.signature: pub func TomlParseFloat(text: char8[..]) -> float64 ! TomlScalarError

doc.summary: Reads a float, including the infinities and NaN that TOML can spell and JSON cannot.
doc.markdown:
Reads a float, including the infinities and NaN that TOML can spell and JSON cannot.
A point needs a digit on either side of it, which is what refuses `.7` and `7.` — both of which some readers
accept and some do not, so a document containing one means different things in different places.
`Malformed` at the first character that cannot be part of the float, `TooLong` past the length bound, and
`OutOfRange` at the start when the digits are a number `float64` cannot hold. Every offset is into `text` as
written, underscores included.
doc.returns: the float, or why it could not be read and where

doc.markdown:
Which of the four date-time shapes a token turned out to be.
There is no case for "not a date-time": text that is none of the four is a failure with a position, not a
fifth shape a caller has to remember to check for before reading the fields beside it.

doc.summary: A date-time as TOML writes it: which of the four shapes it is, and the parts that shape carries.
doc.markdown:
A date-time as TOML writes it: which of the four shapes it is, and the parts that shape carries.
The parts that the shape does not carry are present and meaningless — a `DateOnly` has a time of midnight
because the fields have to hold something — so `shape` is what decides which of them to read. That is why the
shape travels with the value rather than being returned beside it.

items.name: TomlParseDateTime
items.signature: pub func TomlParseDateTime(text: char8[..]) -> TomlDateTime ! TomlScalarError

doc.summary: Reads any of TOML's four date-time forms, reporting which one it was.
doc.markdown:
Reads any of TOML's four date-time forms, reporting which one it was.
The four are genuinely different things and the difference matters: an offset date-time names a moment, and a
local date-time names a reading of a wall clock that different places reach at different moments. Collapsing
them by assuming UTC is how a meeting ends up an hour out, so nothing here supplies an offset that the text
did not.
`Malformed` at the byte where the text stops being one of the four forms — the separator that is not one, the
field the calendar rejects, or the end of the text when it stops early. The calendar's own refusals arrive
here too: the thirty-first of February is four correct digit pairs and not a date.
doc.returns: the date-time and which shape it is, or why it could not be read and where

doc.summary: How long a table's header path may be, in bytes.
doc.markdown:
How long a table's header path may be, in bytes.
A header is written as text, so the path is assembled into a fixed buffer rather than a list of names, and this
is that buffer. It is far past any path a person writes: reaching it takes a nesting of tables whose names add
up to a kilobyte, which a document built in memory can do and one that was parsed effectively cannot.

items.name: TomlWriteDocument
items.signature: pub func TomlWriteDocument(writer: &var TextWriter, table: &TomlValue) -> ! FormatError

doc.summary: Writes `table` as a TOML document.
doc.markdown:
Writes `table` as a TOML document.
The same tree always produces the same bytes, and a document written, read and written again produces the
same bytes the second time — which is what makes this safe to run repeatedly over a file this program owns.
It is not safe in the sense of preserving one it does not: comments, blank lines, indentation and the
spelling of a number are not in the tree, so they cannot come out of it. The output is these values laid out
by this writer, which is an equivalent document and not the same file.
The document is borrowed and nothing is allocated: it writes itself into the destination as it is walked.
Reports whatever the destination reported, unchanged, so a buffer that is merely full stays distinguishable
from a stream that has died — and stops at the first refusal rather than writing the rest of a document into a
destination that has already said no. Reports `ValueOutOfRange` for a table whose header path is longer than
`MaximumHeaderPath`.

params.name: table
params.markdown: the document to write, borrowed for the call

doc.returns: success when the whole document was accepted
